Title: Could Israel’s Palestinians-only death penalty entrench impunity in the West Bank?

Summary: 
Israel’s Knesset has advanced a controversial bill, the Penal Bill (Amendment No. 159) (Death Penalty for Terrorists), which would mandate the death penalty exclusively for Palestinians convicted of terrorism, including those who committed offenses before the law’s enactment. The amendment, proposed by the far-right Jewish Power party led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, passed its first reading with only 39 out of 120 Knesset members voting in favor, raising concerns about democratic legitimacy. The bill would allow military courts in Judea and Samaria (the West Bank) to impose death sentences with a simple majority and prohibit commutation. Human rights organizations, including Amnesty International, B’Tselem, and the International Centre of Justice for Palestinians, have condemned the law as racist, a violation of international human rights law, and a tool to entrench impunity. They highlight the near-99% conviction rate in military courts, systemic denial of medical care in Israeli detention facilities—where at least 94 Palestinians died between October 7, 2023, and August 2025—and the lack of appeal or sentence reduction. The bill follows the summary execution of two surrendering Palestinian men in Jenin on November 27, 2025, which Ben-Gvir publicly endorsed and celebrated. Critics argue the law formalizes existing patterns of lethal force, deepens apartheid-like legal distinctions, and enables state-sanctioned executions while shielding Jewish perpetrators of violence. The bill remains under review by the National Security Committee and must pass two more readings to become law. Meanwhile, several European nations are boycotting the Eurovision Song Contest in Vienna over Israel’s conduct in Gaza, citing the country’s non-compliance with the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits the death penalty.

articles.summary: The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, has urged Israeli authorities to abandon a new bill that would impose mandatory death penalties on Palestinians under certain circumstances, both in occupied Palestinian territories and within Israel. In a statement released on Friday, Türk emphasized that the proposed legislation, along with statements by Israeli politicians, indicates a discriminatory intent targeting Palestinians, who are often convicted in unfair trials. He warned that these measures challenge international law on multiple levels and raise serious concerns about racial discrimination, violations of the right to fair trial, and breaches of international human rights and humanitarian law. Türk underscored that such laws violate international humanitarian law, particularly regarding criminal procedures and the application of the death penalty in occupied territories. He reminded that denying fair trial guarantees to Palestinians from the West Bank and Gaza under the Fourth Geneva Convention constitutes a war crime. The UN clearly opposes the death penalty in all circumstances, citing its incompatibility with human dignity and the irreversible risk of executing innocent people. The proposed Israeli legislation eliminates judicial discretion, violates the right to life, and includes vague definitions such as 'terrorism, racism, or hostility toward the public,' which the UN Human Rights Office deems dangerously ambiguous. These proposals follow several bills introduced before the Israeli Knesset, including amendments to the military law in the West Bank mandating mandatory death sentences for all convicted of premeditated murder, and changes to the Israeli Penal Code to introduce the death penalty for those convicted of intentionally killing Israelis in terrorist acts, with retroactive effect for attacks on October 7, 2023.

articles.title: UN Experts Condemn Israel's Proposed Law on 'Death Penalty for Terrorists'
articles.summary: A group of twelve UN experts has condemned Israel's proposed legislation to impose the death penalty for 'terrorists,' a bill passed in its first reading by the Israeli parliament in November 2025. According to the experts, the law violates the right to life and discriminates against Palestinians. The death penalty has been applied only once in Israeli civilian justice—against Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann in 1962. The proposed law defines the death penalty for anyone who intentionally or recklessly causes the death of an Israeli citizen due to racism or hostility toward a community, with the aim of harming the State of Israel and the renaissance of the Jewish people in their homeland. The experts highlight that the law would apply to a Palestinian killing an Israeli, but not to an Israeli killing a Palestinian, creating a discriminatory framework. They argue that mandatory death penalties violate the right to life and eliminate judicial discretion, preventing courts from considering individual circumstances or mitigating factors. The law would establish two mechanisms: military courts in the occupied West Bank and civilian criminal law in Israel and East Jerusalem, with the death penalty only applicable when intent is proven. The experts, who are UN special rapporteurs and members of the Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances, stress that the law allows death sentences by a simple majority in military courts and prohibits any pardon or commutation, explicitly violating the right to life. The bill still requires second and third readings before becoming law. The Hamas condemned the proposal on November 3, 2025, calling it a 'flagrant violation of international law' and urging the UN and human rights organizations to take immediate action. The Palestinian Authority denounced it as a 'dangerous step toward genocide and ethnic cleansing under the guise of legitimacy.'

articles.title: Knesset Approves First Reading of Law to Prosecute Perpetrators of October 7 Attack
articles.summary: The Israeli Knesset passed the first reading of a bill on January 13, 2026, aimed at prosecuting perpetrators of the October 7, 2023 attack. According to Al Jazeera, the bill was approved unanimously by the Knesset's plenary session with a majority of 19 members. The law establishes a special judicial body chaired by a retired central district court judge to handle proceedings against members of Hamas and its allies involved in the attack, replacing the current regular courts. The special court will have jurisdiction over serious crimes, including genocide, undermining state sovereignty, aiding the enemy during wartime, and terrorism. The law allows deviations from standard criminal procedures and evidence rules to ensure the 'truth' is uncovered, while maintaining trial integrity. Proceedings will be public, broadcast online, and archived by the state. The law permits the death penalty for those convicted of murder and explicitly bans their release in any future prisoner exchanges. A guidance committee, chaired by the Prime Minister and including ministers of justice, defense, and foreign affairs, will determine prosecution policy. The law also mandates that death sentences be carried out by hanging, and that convicted detainees be held in a separate detention facility, with visits restricted to authorized personnel and legal consultations conducted via video only. After the first reading, the bill will be sent to a specialized committee for review and amendments before being voted on in its second and third readings to finalize its text. In December 2025, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu supported the bill, opposing a broader death penalty law proposed by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. In December 2025, the Southern District Attorney, Erez Padan, announced that the prosecution had completed drafting indictment documents against over 300 suspects. However, Israel has not released an official number of detainees or detailed information about individual cases. Since the start of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza over two years ago, thousands of Palestinians have been arrested from Gaza and the West Bank, with most Gaza detainees considered missing due to the lack of information and Israel’s refusal to disclose details.

articles.title: UN Experts Denounce Israel's Proposed Death Penalty Law as Illegal and Discriminatory
articles.summary: Twelve United Nations human rights experts condemned Israel's proposed legislation to impose the death penalty for terrorism-related convictions, declaring it illegal and discriminatory. The experts warned the law would violate the right to life and disproportionately target Palestinians in the occupied territories, citing the existing military legal system in place since 1967, which increases the risk of human rights violations. The proposed law introduces vague and broad definitions of terrorism, including non-genuine terrorist acts, and mandates the death penalty for such crimes without allowing judicial discretion for mitigating circumstances. The experts highlighted a dual legal system: in Israel and East Jerusalem, the death penalty would apply only to intentional killings of Israeli citizens or residents under civilian criminal law, while in the West Bank, military law would apply to any act causing death—intentional or not—targeting Palestinians exclusively. This dual system is deemed discriminatory, as only Palestinians face military tribunals with fewer due process guarantees, while Israeli settlers are exempt. The experts also criticized the prohibition of pardons or commutations, the method of execution by hanging, the short execution timeline (under 90 days), and the secrecy surrounding the process. The statement was signed by UN rapporteurs Francesca Albanese (on Palestine) and Ben Saul (on counter-terrorism and human rights). The bill, an amendment to the Penal Code, remains under legislative review in Israel’s Knesset and has not yet passed all required votes. Israel currently bans the death penalty for most crimes, permitting it only in exceptional cases such as war crimes or genocide; the last execution was Adolf Eichmann in 1962 for crimes against humanity.
